answer: Each block in the rigging is gauged by the rigger and the size is written in the gauge book beside the mast it serves. A umber block claimed as gauged fails the book: the sheave must turn free at the gale of the block, and a block never gauged jams the first time it is hauled. Buying a false gauge record costs a forger 13,700 in bribes to the rigger and fees to the chandler, and the sonnet entry in the book is checked at every refit, so a block whose gauge was never written is cut out of the rig.
